claim: Viruses evolve much more rapidly than host genomes.
source: Host-virus arms races are inherently asymmetric; viruses evolve much more rapidly than host genomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about host-virus evolutionary dynamics.

claim: The APOBEC3 (A3) cytidine deaminases have undergone positive selection.
source: One family of restriction factors, the APOBEC3 (A3) cytidine deaminases, has undergone positive selection and expansion via segmental gene duplication and recombination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the introduction section.

claim: The APOBEC3 (A3) cytidine deaminases have undergone expansion via segmental gene duplication and recombination.
source: One family of restriction factors, the APOBEC3 (A3) cytidine deaminases, has undergone positive selection and expansion via segmental gene duplication and recombination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the introduction section.

claim: All simian primate genomes retain the remnants of an ancient A3 retrocopy called A3I.
source: First, we discovered that all simian primate genomes retain the remnants of an ancient A3 retrocopy: A3I.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some New World monkeys encode up to ten additional APOBEC3G (A3G) retrocopies.
source: Furthermore, we found that some New World monkeys encode up to ten additional APOBEC3G (A3G) retrocopies.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some A3G retrocopies are transcribed in a variety of tissues.
source: Some of these A3G retrocopies are transcribed in a variety of tissues and able to restrict retroviruses.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some A3G retrocopies are able to restrict retroviruses.
source: Some of these A3G retrocopies are transcribed in a variety of tissues and able to restrict retroviruses.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Host genomes co-opt retroelement activity in the germline to create new host restriction factors.
source: Our findings suggest that host genomes co-opt retroelement activity in the germline to create new host restriction factors as another means to keep pace with the rapid evolution of viruses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Endogenous retroelements created a substantial fraction of most animal genomes.
source: One type of these selfish elements, called endogenous retroelements, created a substantial fraction of most animal genomes (Canapa et al., 2016; de Koning et al., 2011; Lander et al., 2001; Smit et al., 2015; Sotero-Caio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Endogenous retroelements can negatively impact host fitness by disrupting genes or regulatory regions.
source: These retroelements can negatively impact host fitness by disrupting genes or regulatory regions, and by increasing the likelihood of ectopic recombination (Boissinot et al., 2001; Hancks and Kazazian, 2012; Kaer and Speek, 2013; Petrov et al., 2003; Song and Boissinot, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Endogenous retroelements can negatively impact host fitness by increasing the likelihood of ectopic recombination.
source: These retroelements can negatively impact host fitness by disrupting genes or regulatory regions, and by increasing the likelihood of ectopic recombination (Boissinot et al., 2001; Hancks and Kazazian, 2012; Kaer and Speek, 2013; Petrov et al., 2003; Song and Boissinot, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: 3,700–18,000 retrocopies are present in the human genome.
source: Previous studies estimated that 3,700–18,000 retrocopies are present in the human genome (Casola and Betrán, 2017; Navarro and Galante, 2015; Potrzebowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retrocopies are intronless and removed from the chromosomal location of the parental intron-containing gene.
source: These 'retrocopies' are intronless and removed from the chromosomal location of the parental intron-containing gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the characteristics of retrocopies.

claim: DNA-based mechanisms of duplication result in a new copy of the gene including its promoter and distal regulatory elements.
source: First, 'DNA-based' mechanisms of duplication (e.g., segmental gene duplications) result in a new copy of the gene including its promoter and distal regulatory elements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA-based gene duplication mechanisms.

claim: Retrocopying typically duplicates only the exons.
source: In contrast, retrocopying typically duplicates only the exons, leading to the moniker 'processed pseudogene'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the characteristics of retrocopying.

claim: Transcription of a new retrocopy depends on the genomic neighborhood into which it integrates.
source: Thus, transcription of a new retrocopy depends on the genomic neighborhood into which it integrates (Carelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Retrocopying relies on the machinery encoded by endogenous retroelements like LINE-1, which are highly active in germline and early embryo.
source: Second, retrocopying relies on the machinery encoded by endogenous retroelements like LINE-1, which are highly active in germline and early embryo (Friedli et al., 2014; Garcia-Perez et al., 2007; Klawitter et al., 2016; Muotri, 2016; Wissing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Retrocopying is almost exclusively limited to RNAs expressed in germline or early embryonic tissues.
source: Therefore, unlike DNA-based duplications, retrocopying is almost exclusively limited to RNAs expressed in germline or early embryonic tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of retrocopying and LINE-1 activity.

claim: The level of germline expression of host mRNAs should be highly correlated to their probability of generating retrocopies.
source: It follows that the level of germline expression of host mRNAs should be highly correlated to their probability of generating retrocopies.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of retrocopying.

claim: Ribosomal proteins represent the most abundant class of processed pseudogenes in the human genome.
source: For example, ribosomal proteins that are highly expressed in germline tissues represent the most abundant class of processed pseudogenes in the human genome (Balasubramanian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The vast majority of retrocopies show characteristic signatures of pseudogenization.
source: While germline expression of host mRNAs predicates the generation of retrocopies, the vast majority of these retrocopies show characteristic signatures of pseudogenization (Casola and Betrán, 2017; Navarro and Galante, 2015; Potrzebowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A subset of retrocopies escaped mutational abrasion, presumably because they provide a selective advantage to the host.
source: While most retrocopies do not increase the genic capacity of the host due to inactivating mutations, a subset of retrocopies escaped mutational abrasion, presumably because they provide a selective advantage to the host.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles and supported by examples in the literature.

claim: Retrocopying of the CypA gene between coding exons of the TRIM5 gene has created novel TRIMCyp fusion genes that can potently restrict retroviruses including HIV-1.
source: For example, retrocopying of the CypA gene between coding exons of the TRIM5 gene has created novel TRIMCyp fusion genes that can potently restrict retroviruses including HIV-1 (Malfavon-Borja et al., 2013; Newman et al., 2008; Nisole et al., 2004; Sayah et al., 2004; Virgen et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Retrocopying has created TRIMCyp fusion genes multiple times during primate evolution.
source: In a remarkable case of convergent evolution, retrocopying has created TRIMCyp fusion genes multiple times during primate evolution, further expanding and diversifying the TRIM gene family for retroviral defense (Brennan et al., 2008; Virgen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The common ancestor of placental mammals likely encoded three A3 genes.
source: Although the common ancestor of placental mammals likely encoded three A3 genes (Münk et al., 2012), this locus has recurrently expanded and contracted throughout mammalian evolution (Ito et al., 2020), including a dramatic expansion to seven paralogous genes in catarrhine primates (Old World monkeys and hominoids) followed by recurrent positive selection of this expanded gene set (Bulliard et al., 2009; Compton et al., 2012; Duggal et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2012; McLaughlin et al., 2016; OhAinle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The A3 locus has recurrently expanded and contracted throughout mammalian evolution.
source: Although the common ancestor of placental mammals likely encoded three A3 genes (Münk et al., 2012), this locus has recurrently expanded and contracted throughout mammalian evolution (Ito et al., 2020), including a dramatic expansion to seven paralogous genes in catarrhine primates (Old World monkeys and hominoids) followed by recurrent positive selection of this expanded gene set (Bulliard et al., 2009; Compton et al., 2012; Duggal et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2012; McLaughlin et al., 2016; OhAinle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There was a dramatic expansion to seven paralogous A3 genes in catarrhine primates (Old World monkeys and hominoids).
source: Although the common ancestor of placental mammals likely encoded three A3 genes (Münk et al., 2012), this locus has recurrently expanded and contracted throughout mammalian evolution (Ito et al., 2020), including a dramatic expansion to seven paralogous genes in catarrhine primates (Old World monkeys and hominoids) followed by recurrent positive selection of this expanded gene set (Bulliard et al., 2009; Compton et al., 2012; Duggal et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2012; McLaughlin et al., 2016; OhAinle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The expanded A3 gene set in catarrhine primates underwent recurrent positive selection.
source: Although the common ancestor of placental mammals likely encoded three A3 genes (Münk et al., 2012), this locus has recurrently expanded and contracted throughout mammalian evolution (Ito et al., 2020), including a dramatic expansion to seven paralogous genes in catarrhine primates (Old World monkeys and hominoids) followed by recurrent positive selection of this expanded gene set (Bulliard et al., 2009; Compton et al., 2012; Duggal et al., 2011; Henry et al., 2012; McLaughlin et al., 2016; OhAinle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ancient and recent retrocopying has further diversified the A3 gene repertoire in primates, adding as many as ten new A3s outside the A3 locus.
source: We found that ancient and recent retrocopying has further diversified the already expansive A3 gene repertoire in primates, adding as many as ten new A3s outside the well-studied' A3 locus'.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A3I is an ancient A3 born via retrocopying in the common ancestor of simian primates.
source: Our work uncovered an ancient A3 born via retrocopying in the common ancestor of simian primates and a dramatic, ongoing history of A3 retrocopying in New World monkeys (NWMs).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic and genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a dramatic, ongoing history of A3 retrocopying in New World monkeys (NWMs).
source: Our work uncovered an ancient A3 born via retrocopying in the common ancestor of simian primates and a dramatic, ongoing history of A3 retrocopying in New World monkeys (NWMs).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Retrocopied A3s have continually expanded host defense repertoires in primate genomes.
source: Thus, retrocopied A3s have continually expanded host defense repertoires in primate genomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The A3 locus of human, other hominoids, and Old World monkeys comprises seven clustered genes, A3A-A3H.
source: The A3 locus of human, other hominoids, and Old World monkeys comprises seven clustered genes, A3A-A3H (Jarmuz et al., 2002; OhAinle et al., 2006; Silvas and Schiffer, 2019; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In every simian primate genome examined, there is exactly one shared syntenic region, distinct from the A3 locus, with high similarity to A3G.
source: However, in every simian primate genome examined, we also found exactly one shared syntenic region, distinct from the A3 locus, with high similarity to A3G.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The A3I sequence match spans the exonic sequences of A3G in a single contiguous region of around 1,100 bp.
source: This sequence match spanned the exonic sequences of A3G in a single contiguous region of around 1,100 bp (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A3I is a retrocopy of an A3 gene based on the absence of introns.
source: Based on the absence of introns, we concluded that this sequence represents a retrocopy of an A3 gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural characteristics of the sequence.

claim: There is no evidence of the syntenic copy of A3I in the genomes of prosimians including the tarsier, bushbaby, and mouse lemur.
source: We found no evidence of the syntenic copy of this A3 retrocopy in the genomes of prosimians including the tarsier, bushbaby, and mouse lemur.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A3I was born in the common ancestor of simian primates.
source: We, therefore, conclude that this retrocopy was born in the common ancestor of simian primates, and hence propose the name A3I for this retrocopy, extending the nomenclature scheme for other human A3 genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on phylogenetic and genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All A3Is share a common ancestor to the exclusion of A3B and A3G genes.
source: With high bootstrap support, we found that all A3Is share a common ancestor to the exclusion of A3B and A3G genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A3G genes are the closest phylogenetic neighbors of the A3Is.
source: Our analyses found the A3G genes to be the closest phylogenetic neighbors of the A3Is, suggesting a common ancestry of these two genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic analysis data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A3G is predicted to have been born soon after the simian-prosimian split.
source: Since A3G is predicted to have been born soon after the simian-prosimian split (Münk et al., 2012), we propose that A3I arose via retrocopying of A3G in the common ancestor of simian primates, approximately 43 million years ago (MYA) (Perelman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A3I arose via retrocopying of A3G in the common ancestor of simian primates, approximately 43 million years ago (MYA).
source: Since A3G is predicted to have been born soon after the simian-prosimian split (Münk et al., 2012), we propose that A3I arose via retrocopying of A3G in the common ancestor of simian primates, approximately 43 million years ago (MYA) (Perelman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on phylogenetic analysis and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All A3I retrocopies share a nonsense mutation at codon position 261.
source: We found that all A3I retrocopies share a nonsense mutation at codon position 261 (Supplementary file 3), and thus, in most species, A3I encodes only a short putative open reading frame (ORF) of 153 codons (compared to the 384 codon ORF of A3G) which spans the N-terminal deaminase domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In most species, A3I encodes only a short putative open reading frame (ORF) of 153 codons.
source: We found that all A3I retrocopies share a nonsense mutation at codon position 261 (Supplementary file 3), and thus, in most species, A3I encodes only a short putative open reading frame (ORF) of 153 codons (compared to the 384 codon ORF of A3G) which spans the N-terminal deaminase domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A3G encodes a 384 codon ORF.

claim: There were additional lineage-specific disruptions of the A3I ORF during the diversification of simian primates.
source: Following this initial truncation, there were additional lineage-specific disruptions of the A3I ORF during the diversification of simian primates.

claim: A3I was born in the simian ancestor either as a truncated retrocopy or acquired a truncating mutation shortly following birth.
source: These results suggest that A3I was born in the simian ancestor either as a truncated retrocopy or acquired a truncating mutation shortly following birth.

source: Our analyses also revealed A3F retrocopies in three Old World monkeys within the Colobinae subfamily, A3H retrocopies in two New World monkeys, and a single A3 retrocopy that cannot be assigned to a specific A3 parent in the greater galago (Otolemur garnettii) (Figure 1D).

claim: There are A3H retrocopies in two New World monkeys.

claim: There is a single A3 retrocopy that cannot be assigned to a specific A3 parent in the greater galago (Otolemur garnettii).
source: Our analyses also revealed A3F retrocopies in three Old World monkeys within the Colobinae subfamily, A3H retrocopies in two New World monkeys, and a single A3 retrocopy that cannot be assigned to a specific A3 parent in the greater galago (Otolemur garnettii) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic analysis data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Every sequenced NWM genome contains numerous A3G retrocopies.
source: However, our most striking finding was that every sequenced NWM genome contained numerous A3G retrocopies.

claim: The three intron-containing A3 genes in marmoset are likely orthologous to human A3A, A3G, and A3H.

Like marmoset, we found multiple A3G retrocopies in each of these genomes – eight in capuchin, seven in night monkey, and ten in squirrel monkey (Figure 2A).

claim: The white-faced capuchin genome contains eight A3G retrocopies.

claim: Five clusters of A3G retrocopies represent orthologs born in or before the last common ancestor of the four analyzed NWM species.

claim: Five orthologous NWM A3G retrocopies were likely born via independent retrotransposition events in or prior to the most recent common ancestor of the four analyzed species.

claim: Retrocopies C1, C2, C3, and C5 of marmoset are present in titi (Plecturocebus moloch) and saki monkeys (Pithecia pithecia).

claim: Retrocopies C1, C2, C3, and C5 were born in or prior to the most recent common ancestor of all NWMs (~25 MYA).

claim: Species-specific A3G retrocopies share a recent common ancestor with the intron-containing A3G gene from the same species.

claim: Some 'marmoset-specific' retrocopies are also present in the closely related tamarin (Saguinus oedipus).

claim: A3G retrocopies vary in age, from being found in only one species, in a few closely related species, in all NWM species, or in all simian primates.
source: Thus, A3G retrocopies vary in age, from being found in only one species, in a few closely related species, in all NWM species, or in all simian primates.

claim: A3G retrocopies have been continually born throughout the evolutionary history of NWMs.
